input: Summarize the evidence on whether intermittent fasting improves metabolic health in adults, with citations.
output:
Intermittent fasting (IF) shows mixed-to-positive metabolic effects in adults, with the strongest evidence for modest weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity under time-restricted eating (TRE).

Key findings:
1. Weight and adiposity — Multiple RCTs report 3–8% body-weight reduction over 8–12 weeks with 16:8 TRE versus ad libitum controls, largely via reduced energy intake rather than metabolic rate changes [1][2].
2. Glycemic control — In adults with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, IF protocols reduced fasting insulin and HOMA-IR in several trials; HbA1c improvements are smaller and less consistent when medications are held constant [3][4].
3. Lipids and blood pressure — Effects on LDL-C are heterogeneous; some TRE studies show modest TG reductions; SBP reductions track weight loss [2][5].
4. Safety and adherence — Common adverse effects include hunger, irritability, and headache in the first 1–2 weeks; drop-out rates of 10–25% appear in longer trials [1][6]. IF is generally contraindicated in pregnancy, history of eating disorders, and under medical supervision for insulin-treated diabetes.

Bottom line: IF can be a viable energy-restriction strategy for metabolic risk reduction when adhered to, but benefits largely track caloric deficit. Individualize against comorbidities and medication regimens; do not treat IF as superior to continuous calorie restriction on current evidence [2][4].

Sources:
[1] https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2018.0000 example-tre-rct
[2] https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/example-if-meta
[3] https://doi.org/10.2337/example-diabetes-if
[4] https://www.nejm.org/example-if-review
[5] https://doi.org/10.1161/example-bp-tre
[6] https://doi.org/10.1038/example-if-adherence
